event_description: State of emergency for arctic cold and dangerous wind chills, so heating fuel deliveries could continue
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An arctic cold front moved through Northern New England on the afternoon of Jan. 13.  Arctic high pressure settled southeast from Central Canada Jan. 14 through Jan. 16.  Wind chill values of 33 to 50 degrees below zero were recorded during the peak of this outbreak on the morning of Jan. 15.

event_description: State of emergency for arctic cold and dangerous wind chills, so heating fuel deliveries could continue
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure intensifying across the maritime provinces drew arctic air across the region. Sustained winds of 20 to 30 mph...with gusts to 40 mph at times...developed between the intense maritimes low and arctic high pressure to the west drawing the arctic air across the region and producing dangerous wind chills. The winds combined with low temperatures of 15 to 30 below zero across northern areas and lows of 10 to 20 below zero Downeast to frequently produce wind chills of 45 to 65 below zero across northern areas with wind chills of 35 to 55 below zero Downeast. Temperatures remained below zero across northern areas during this time. High temperatures on the 15th only reached 10 to 15 below zero across northern areas...barely reaching zero along the Downeast coast. The extreme wind chills prompted many schools to close and resulted in the cancellation of events...particularly across northern portions of the region.

event_description: Emergency proclamation for arctic cold and dangerous wind chills, so heating oil deliveries could continue
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapidly intensifying low pressure tracking just east of the Gulf of Maine brought blizzard conditions to Downeast Maine. Storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 7 to 12 inches across coastal Washington county...with localized totals to around 17 inches. Across coastal Hancock county storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 4 to 10 inches with the greatest accumulations across eastern areas. Storm total snow accumulations across interior Downeast areas generally ranged from 4 to 7 inches. Wind gusts of 40 to 60 mph were reported along the coast...with gusts of 30 to 45 mph across interior areas. The winds produced extensive blowing and drifting snow...with drifts several feet deep reported...along with near zero visibilities at times. The strong winds also contributed to sporadic power outages. Some roads were nearly impassible at times during the storm due to the heavy snow rates...drifting and reduced visibilities. Many events were cancelled due to the storm.

event_description: State of emergency for a severe wind storm that left thousands without power
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High winds knocked over trees which caused damage and power outages across the area.  About 60,000 customers served by Central Maine Power Company lost electrical service during the event.  Trees were reported down in central and southern Somerset County; a plane blew over in Kennebec County; trees fell onto a houses in Cape Neddick in York County and Scarborough in Cumberland County, and a 30x60 ft shed was moved about 60 ft in Lincoln County.

event_description: State of emergency for a severe wind storm that left thousands without power
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong damaging winds developed in advance of a cold front associated with rapidly intensifying low pressure tracking northeast through Quebec province. Sustained south to southeast winds of 30 to 40 mph...with gusts of 50 to 60 mph...persisted for several hours. Significant tree damage was reported across the entire region...with many trees snapped or uprooted. Wet ground conditions and the extended duration of the strong winds contributed to the significant tree damage. Many trees and branches fell on powerlines which either brought down the powerlines or snapped utility poles. Other uitility poles were blown over or snapped by the strong winds. Tens of thousands of customers lost power for varying lengths of time during the storm. Fallen trees and powerlines blocked some roads. In Milo...a large shed was flipped over by the winds. Damage to signs...building siding and roof shingles was reported across the entire region.

event_description: Statewide state of emergency for the Patriots' Day Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure rapidly intensified while tracking from the southeastern states to the southern New England coast from the 15th to the 16th. A tight pressure gradient developed between the low and high pressure centered over eastern Canada which also blocked the northern movement of the low. The intense low slowly drifted east from the 16th through the 19th while high pressure remained across eastern Canada. The storm had many impacts on the region including strong damaging winds...heavy rain with urban and small stream flooding and coastal tidal flooding. These impacts were most significant across Downeast areas...particularly near the coast. In addition...the storm brought locally heavy snow to some higher elevations of northern and northwest Maine.|The tight pressure gradient supported strong east to northeast winds across mostly central and Downeast portions of the region through the 16th and 17th. Disturbances rotating around the main low contributed to several surges of strong winds over the course of the event. Winds gradually diminished during the 18th and 19th...though gusty winds still lingered during this time particularly near the Downeast coast.|Damaging winds occurred across all of Downeast Maine...particularly near the coast where some wind gusts exceeded 70 mph. Damaging winds extended inland to central Piscataquis...central Penobscot and northern Washington counties. The combination of strong winds and saturated ground from the heavy rains which accompanied the storm and the spring thaw contributed to the uprooting of numerous trees with many other trees snapped and broken. Several trees fell on structures and vehicles causing damage. Other trees and branches brought down powerlines when they fell...with power poles also snapped and toppled due to the strong winds which contributed to thousands of power outages. Fallen trees and power lines also blocked roads.|The combination of astronomical high tides...amongst the highest of the year...along with persistent strong onshore winds and large waves contributed to coastal flooding during high tide cycles starting on the evening of the 16th and continuing through the evening of the 19th. During high tides...overwash flooded some coastal roads resulting in road closures. Debris was washed onto roads with some roads also damaged. A causeway connecting the mainland with Deer Isle was closed several times during the event due to overwash and flooding.|The storm also brought heavy rain to the region. The heaviest rains occurred across central and Downeast areas...along with the favored upslope areas of Piscataquis county. Rainfall totals across central and Downeast areas generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches...with local totals in excess of 5.00 inches. Across Piscataquis county...rainfall totals generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches with local totals approaching 5.00 inches. The heavy rain contributed to rapid rises on smaller rivers and streams across the region some of which overflowed onto surrounding low land areas. The small river and stream flooding caused some road closures. Urban and poor drainage flooding also occurred which led to additional road closures and contributed to basement flooding. Mainstem rivers also rose during this time but crested below flood stage.|Enough cold air was in place to support an interval of heavy snow during the early stages of the event across the higher terrain of Piscataquis county and northern Somerset county. Snowfall totals across some higher terrain areas ranged from 8 to 12 inches...with local totals in excess of 12 inches. Lesser snow acumulations occurred at lower elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The storm brought heavy rain to the region. Storm total rainfall across the county generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches...with local totals between 5.00 and 6.00 inches. Minor flooding began to develop during the morning of the 16th...with more extensive flooding developing that evening. The heavy rains caused rapid rises on smaller rivers and streams...some of which overflowed. Flooding of smaller rivers and streams...along with poor drainage and lowland flooding occurred across the entire county. Flooding led to the closure of many roads across the county. Road closures and flooding were reported at Route 166 in Castine...Route 230 in Trenton...portions of Route 1A in Ellsworth...Route 204 in Lamoine at Archers Brook and Fly Point Road in Brooklin. Road closures were also reported on Mount Desert Island including Route 3 at Seal Harbor...Bettys Road and Gilbert Farm Road near Bar Harbor along with Route 102 and Seawall Road at Southwest Harbor. Coastal flooding also contributed to the closure of some roads on Mount Desert Island. The flooding damaged some roads and bridges. Some basements were also flooded. The larger mainstem rivers rose...but crested below flood stage.|

event_description: Statewide state of emergency for the Patriots' Day Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure rapidly intensified while tracking from the southeastern states to the southern New England coast from the 15th to the 16th. A tight pressure gradient developed between the low and high pressure centered over eastern Canada which also blocked the northern movement of the low. The intense low slowly drifted east from the 16th through the 19th while high pressure remained across eastern Canada. The storm had many impacts on the region including strong damaging winds...heavy rain with urban and small stream flooding and coastal tidal flooding. These impacts were most significant across Downeast areas...particularly near the coast. In addition...the storm brought locally heavy snow to some higher elevations of northern and northwest Maine.|The tight pressure gradient supported strong east to northeast winds across mostly central and Downeast portions of the region through the 16th and 17th. Disturbances rotating around the main low contributed to several surges of strong winds over the course of the event. Winds gradually diminished during the 18th and 19th...though gusty winds still lingered during this time particularly near the Downeast coast.|Damaging winds occurred across all of Downeast Maine...particularly near the coast where some wind gusts exceeded 70 mph. Damaging winds extended inland to central Piscataquis...central Penobscot and northern Washington counties. The combination of strong winds and saturated ground from the heavy rains which accompanied the storm and the spring thaw contributed to the uprooting of numerous trees with many other trees snapped and broken. Several trees fell on structures and vehicles causing damage. Other trees and branches brought down powerlines when they fell...with power poles also snapped and toppled due to the strong winds which contributed to thousands of power outages. Fallen trees and power lines also blocked roads.|The combination of astronomical high tides...amongst the highest of the year...along with persistent strong onshore winds and large waves contributed to coastal flooding during high tide cycles starting on the evening of the 16th and continuing through the evening of the 19th. During high tides...overwash flooded some coastal roads resulting in road closures. Debris was washed onto roads with some roads also damaged. A causeway connecting the mainland with Deer Isle was closed several times during the event due to overwash and flooding.|The storm also brought heavy rain to the region. The heaviest rains occurred across central and Downeast areas...along with the favored upslope areas of Piscataquis county. Rainfall totals across central and Downeast areas generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches...with local totals in excess of 5.00 inches. Across Piscataquis county...rainfall totals generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches with local totals approaching 5.00 inches. The heavy rain contributed to rapid rises on smaller rivers and streams across the region some of which overflowed onto surrounding low land areas. The small river and stream flooding caused some road closures. Urban and poor drainage flooding also occurred which led to additional road closures and contributed to basement flooding. Mainstem rivers also rose during this time but crested below flood stage.|Enough cold air was in place to support an interval of heavy snow during the early stages of the event across the higher terrain of Piscataquis county and northern Somerset county. Snowfall totals across some higher terrain areas ranged from 8 to 12 inches...with local totals in excess of 12 inches. Lesser snow acumulations occurred at lower elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The storm brought heavy rain to the region...particularly across southern portions of the county. Storm total rainfall across the county generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches...with local totals between 5.00 and 6.00 inches. The heaviest rains fell across southern portions of the county where the flooding was reported. Minor flooding began to develop during the morning of the 16th...with more extensive flooding developing that evening. The heavy rains caused rapid rises on smaller rivers and streams...some of which overflowed. Flooding of smaller rivers and streams...along with poor drainage and lowland flooding led to the closure of many roads across southern portions of the county. Road closures and flooding were reported at Stillwater Avenue in Orono...Route 143 in Old Town...Valley Road in Exeter near Routes 11/43...Route 169 and West Plymouth Road in Etna and Route 143 in Carmel near I-95. The flooding damaged some roads and bridges. Many basements were also flooded. The larger mainstem rivers rose...but crested below flood stage.

event_description: Statewide state of emergency for the Patriots' Day Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure rapidly intensified while tracking from the southeastern states to the southern New England coast from the 15th to the 16th. A tight pressure gradient developed between the low and high pressure centered over eastern Canada which also blocked the northern movement of the low. The intense low slowly drifted east from the 16th through the 19th while high pressure remained across eastern Canada. The storm had many impacts on the region including strong damaging winds...heavy rain with urban and small stream flooding and coastal tidal flooding. These impacts were most significant across Downeast areas...particularly near the coast. In addition...the storm brought locally heavy snow to some higher elevations of northern and northwest Maine.|The tight pressure gradient supported strong east to northeast winds across mostly central and Downeast portions of the region through the 16th and 17th. Disturbances rotating around the main low contributed to several surges of strong winds over the course of the event. Winds gradually diminished during the 18th and 19th...though gusty winds still lingered during this time particularly near the Downeast coast.|Damaging winds occurred across all of Downeast Maine...particularly near the coast where some wind gusts exceeded 70 mph. Damaging winds extended inland to central Piscataquis...central Penobscot and northern Washington counties. The combination of strong winds and saturated ground from the heavy rains which accompanied the storm and the spring thaw contributed to the uprooting of numerous trees with many other trees snapped and broken. Several trees fell on structures and vehicles causing damage. Other trees and branches brought down powerlines when they fell...with power poles also snapped and toppled due to the strong winds which contributed to thousands of power outages. Fallen trees and power lines also blocked roads.|The combination of astronomical high tides...amongst the highest of the year...along with persistent strong onshore winds and large waves contributed to coastal flooding during high tide cycles starting on the evening of the 16th and continuing through the evening of the 19th. During high tides...overwash flooded some coastal roads resulting in road closures. Debris was washed onto roads with some roads also damaged. A causeway connecting the mainland with Deer Isle was closed several times during the event due to overwash and flooding.|The storm also brought heavy rain to the region. The heaviest rains occurred across central and Downeast areas...along with the favored upslope areas of Piscataquis county. Rainfall totals across central and Downeast areas generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches...with local totals in excess of 5.00 inches. Across Piscataquis county...rainfall totals generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches with local totals approaching 5.00 inches. The heavy rain contributed to rapid rises on smaller rivers and streams across the region some of which overflowed onto surrounding low land areas. The small river and stream flooding caused some road closures. Urban and poor drainage flooding also occurred which led to additional road closures and contributed to basement flooding. Mainstem rivers also rose during this time but crested below flood stage.|Enough cold air was in place to support an interval of heavy snow during the early stages of the event across the higher terrain of Piscataquis county and northern Somerset county. Snowfall totals across some higher terrain areas ranged from 8 to 12 inches...with local totals in excess of 12 inches. Lesser snow acumulations occurred at lower elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds uprooted or broke trees...along with snapping many branches across the region. Wind gusts of 35 to 45 mph were common...with some gusts to around 60 mph. Nearly two dozen trees were uprooted in the Springfield area alone over the course of the storm. The uprooted trees and snapped branches falling on power lines...with some utility poles also toppled due to the winds...contributed to power outages.

Damage to marinas, buoys, docks and coastal property was significant. Channel markers went adrift from their 20,000 pound blocks, causing navigation problems for mariners. The Portland Large Navigational buoy was heavily damaged while measuring 32 foot waves and was later found drifting near the Isles of Shoals. Water and waves were over the roads along the coast, including Saco and York.

event_description: Statewide state of emergency for the Patriots' Day Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure rapidly intensified while tracking from the southeastern states to the southern New England coast from the 15th to the 16th. A tight pressure gradient developed between the low and high pressure centered over eastern Canada which also blocked the northern movement of the low. The intense low slowly drifted east from the 16th through the 19th while high pressure remained across eastern Canada. The storm had many impacts on the region including strong damaging winds...heavy rain with urban and small stream flooding and coastal tidal flooding. These impacts were most significant across Downeast areas...particularly near the coast. In addition...the storm brought locally heavy snow to some higher elevations of northern and northwest Maine.|The tight pressure gradient supported strong east to northeast winds across mostly central and Downeast portions of the region through the 16th and 17th. Disturbances rotating around the main low contributed to several surges of strong winds over the course of the event. Winds gradually diminished during the 18th and 19th...though gusty winds still lingered during this time particularly near the Downeast coast.|Damaging winds occurred across all of Downeast Maine...particularly near the coast where some wind gusts exceeded 70 mph. Damaging winds extended inland to central Piscataquis...central Penobscot and northern Washington counties. The combination of strong winds and saturated ground from the heavy rains which accompanied the storm and the spring thaw contributed to the uprooting of numerous trees with many other trees snapped and broken. Several trees fell on structures and vehicles causing damage. Other trees and branches brought down powerlines when they fell...with power poles also snapped and toppled due to the strong winds which contributed to thousands of power outages. Fallen trees and power lines also blocked roads.|The combination of astronomical high tides...amongst the highest of the year...along with persistent strong onshore winds and large waves contributed to coastal flooding during high tide cycles starting on the evening of the 16th and continuing through the evening of the 19th. During high tides...overwash flooded some coastal roads resulting in road closures. Debris was washed onto roads with some roads also damaged. A causeway connecting the mainland with Deer Isle was closed several times during the event due to overwash and flooding.|The storm also brought heavy rain to the region. The heaviest rains occurred across central and Downeast areas...along with the favored upslope areas of Piscataquis county. Rainfall totals across central and Downeast areas generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches...with local totals in excess of 5.00 inches. Across Piscataquis county...rainfall totals generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches with local totals approaching 5.00 inches. The heavy rain contributed to rapid rises on smaller rivers and streams across the region some of which overflowed onto surrounding low land areas. The small river and stream flooding caused some road closures. Urban and poor drainage flooding also occurred which led to additional road closures and contributed to basement flooding. Mainstem rivers also rose during this time but crested below flood stage.|Enough cold air was in place to support an interval of heavy snow during the early stages of the event across the higher terrain of Piscataquis county and northern Somerset county. Snowfall totals across some higher terrain areas ranged from 8 to 12 inches...with local totals in excess of 12 inches. Lesser snow acumulations occurred at lower elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds uprooted or broke numerous trees...along with snapping many branches across the region. Wind gusts of 55 to 65 mph were common...with some gusts to around 70 mph near the immediate coast.|Some measured gusts included 71 mph at Brooklin...64 mph at Prospect Harbor...63 mph at Naskeag Point...62 mph at Stonington...57 mph at Sedgwick and 53 mph at Bar Harbor. Several intervals of particularly strong winds occurred. The first episode of stronger winds occurred during the afternoon of the 16th which produced the initial wind damage. The second episode of stronger winds...generally the strongest of the event...occurred during the night of the 16th producing further damage. The third episode of particularly strong winds occurred during the afternoon of the 17th. The numerous uprooted trees and snapped branches falling on power lines...with many utility poles also toppled due to the winds...contributed to extensive power outages. Many roads were blocked due to fallen trees...utility poles and power lines. Tree damage was particularly extensive across Mount Desert Island and Acadia National Park. Structural damage to homes due to falling trees was reported at Gouldsboro...Swans Island and on Mount Desert Island. Many structures also suffered various degrees of damage to roofs and siding...with many signs also damaged. In both Sedgwick and Deer Isle...a tree fell on vehicles with no injuries reported. Several harbors suffered damage to piers and docks due to the strong winds and rough seas.

event_description: Statewide state of emergency for the Patriots' Day Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure rapidly intensified while tracking from the southeastern states to the southern New England coast from the 15th to the 16th. A tight pressure gradient developed between the low and high pressure centered over eastern Canada which also blocked the northern movement of the low. The intense low slowly drifted east from the 16th through the 19th while high pressure remained across eastern Canada. The storm had many impacts on the region including strong damaging winds...heavy rain with urban and small stream flooding and coastal tidal flooding. These impacts were most significant across Downeast areas...particularly near the coast. In addition...the storm brought locally heavy snow to some higher elevations of northern and northwest Maine.|The tight pressure gradient supported strong east to northeast winds across mostly central and Downeast portions of the region through the 16th and 17th. Disturbances rotating around the main low contributed to several surges of strong winds over the course of the event. Winds gradually diminished during the 18th and 19th...though gusty winds still lingered during this time particularly near the Downeast coast.|Damaging winds occurred across all of Downeast Maine...particularly near the coast where some wind gusts exceeded 70 mph. Damaging winds extended inland to central Piscataquis...central Penobscot and northern Washington counties. The combination of strong winds and saturated ground from the heavy rains which accompanied the storm and the spring thaw contributed to the uprooting of numerous trees with many other trees snapped and broken. Several trees fell on structures and vehicles causing damage. Other trees and branches brought down powerlines when they fell...with power poles also snapped and toppled due to the strong winds which contributed to thousands of power outages. Fallen trees and power lines also blocked roads.|The combination of astronomical high tides...amongst the highest of the year...along with persistent strong onshore winds and large waves contributed to coastal flooding during high tide cycles starting on the evening of the 16th and continuing through the evening of the 19th. During high tides...overwash flooded some coastal roads resulting in road closures. Debris was washed onto roads with some roads also damaged. A causeway connecting the mainland with Deer Isle was closed several times during the event due to overwash and flooding.|The storm also brought heavy rain to the region. The heaviest rains occurred across central and Downeast areas...along with the favored upslope areas of Piscataquis county. Rainfall totals across central and Downeast areas generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches...with local totals in excess of 5.00 inches. Across Piscataquis county...rainfall totals generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches with local totals approaching 5.00 inches. The heavy rain contributed to rapid rises on smaller rivers and streams across the region some of which overflowed onto surrounding low land areas. The small river and stream flooding caused some road closures. Urban and poor drainage flooding also occurred which led to additional road closures and contributed to basement flooding. Mainstem rivers also rose during this time but crested below flood stage.|Enough cold air was in place to support an interval of heavy snow during the early stages of the event across the higher terrain of Piscataquis county and northern Somerset county. Snowfall totals across some higher terrain areas ranged from 8 to 12 inches...with local totals in excess of 12 inches. Lesser snow acumulations occurred at lower elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds uprooted or broke numerous trees...along with snapping many branches across the region. Wind gusts of 55 to 65 mph were common...with some gusts to around 70 mph near the immediate coast.|Some measured gusts included 72 mph at Cutler...53 mph at Eastport|and 48 mph at Milbridge. Several intervals of particularly strong winds occurred. The first episode of stronger winds occurred during the afternoon of the 16th which produced the initial wind damage. The second episode of stronger winds...generally the strongest of the event...occurred during the night of the 16th producing further damage. The third episode of particularly strong winds occurred during the afternoon of the 17th. The numerous uprooted trees and snapped branches falling on power lines...with many utility poles also toppled due to the winds...contributed to extensive power outages. Many roads were blocked due to fallen trees...utility poles and power lines.  Structural damage occurred to homes due to falling trees. Many structures also suffered various degrees of damage to roofs and siding...with many signs also damaged. In Eastport windows were blown out of several buildings along the waterfront during the evening of the 16th. A roof was torn off a mobile home in Lubec. Several harbors suffered damage to piers and docks due to the strong winds and rough seas.

A tight pressure gradient developed between the low and high pressure centered over eastern Canada which also blocked the northern movement of the low. The intense low slowly drifted east from the 16th through the 19th while high pressure remained across eastern Canada. The storm had many impacts on the region including strong damaging winds...heavy rain with urban and small stream flooding and coastal tidal flooding. These impacts were most significant across Downeast areas...particularly near the coast. In addition...the storm brought locally heavy snow to some higher elevations of northern and northwest Maine.|The tight pressure gradient supported strong east to northeast winds across mostly central and Downeast portions of the region through the 16th and 17th. Disturbances rotating around the main low contributed to several surges of strong winds over the course of the event. Winds gradually diminished during the 18th and 19th...though gusty winds still lingered during this time particularly near the Downeast coast.|Damaging winds occurred across all of Downeast Maine...particularly near the coast where some wind gusts exceeded 70 mph. Damaging winds extended inland to central Piscataquis...central Penobscot and northern Washington counties. The combination of strong winds and saturated ground from the heavy rains which accompanied the storm and the spring thaw contributed to the uprooting of numerous trees with many other trees snapped and broken. Several trees fell on structures and vehicles causing damage. Other trees and branches brought down powerlines when they fell...with power poles also snapped and toppled due to the strong winds which contributed to thousands of power outages. Fallen trees and power lines also blocked roads.|The combination of astronomical high tides...amongst the highest of the year...along with persistent strong onshore winds and large waves contributed to coastal flooding during high tide cycles starting on the evening of the 16th and continuing through the evening of the 19th. During high tides...overwash flooded some coastal roads resulting in road closures. Debris was washed onto roads with some roads also damaged. A causeway connecting the mainland with Deer Isle was closed several times during the event due to overwash and flooding.|The storm also brought heavy rain to the region. The heaviest rains occurred across central and Downeast areas...along with the favored upslope areas of Piscataquis county. Rainfall totals across central and Downeast areas generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches...with local totals in excess of 5.00 inches. Across Piscataquis county...rainfall totals generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches with local totals approaching 5.00 inches. The heavy rain contributed to rapid rises on smaller rivers and streams across the region some of which overflowed onto surrounding low land areas. The small river and stream flooding caused some road closures. Urban and poor drainage flooding also occurred which led to additional road closures and contributed to basement flooding. Mainstem rivers also rose during this time but crested below flood stage.|Enough cold air was in place to support an interval of heavy snow during the early stages of the event across the higher terrain of Piscataquis county and northern Somerset county. Snowfall totals across some higher terrain areas ranged from 8 to 12 inches...with local totals in excess of 12 inches. Lesser snow acumulations occurred at lower elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of astronomical high tides...among the highest of the year...persistent onshore winds and large waves contributed to coastal flooding during high tide cycles from the evening of the 16th through the early morning hours of the 19th. During high tide...overwash and flooding closed several coastal roads and parking areas. Coastal roads were covered with debris and in some cases damaged.

event_description: Statewide state of emergency for the Patriots' Day Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure over the southeastern United States on the morning of Sunday, April 15th, rapidly intensified as it slowly moved north to near New York City by the morning of Monday, April 16th. This intense low in combination with high pressure over eastern Canada produced Overview: An area of low pressure intensified rapidly as it moved slowly from the southeastern United States on the morning of Sunday, April 15th to near New York City by the morning of Monday, April 16th.  The intense low over New York City in combination with high pressure over eastern Canada produced a very intense pressure gradient across the area which caused strong east to northeast winds to develop across the region.  Over land, the strong winds downed numerous trees.  The downed trees caused widespread power outages, especially near the coast, and numerous road closures.  Over the marine areas, the strong winds caused a storm surge and large ocean waves of up to 30 feet to develop.  The combination of astronomical high tides, storm surge, and large waves contributed to coastal flooding in coastal areas of the state and severe coastal erosion in areas south of Portland.|The storm also brought heavy rain to the region which, when combined with snow melt, produced widespread flooding across much of the region.  The flooding of small rivers and streams was worst in southern and coastal areas and led to numerous road closures.   In the mountains, the rain was preceded by heavy snow.  Flooding was minor on most mainstem rivers, however, in southern Maine, the Presumpscot River reached near record levels. |The intense low drifted very slowly eastward from Monday morning through Friday morning as it gradually weakened.  During this time, the pressure gradient slowly relaxed, the winds gradually diminished, and the seas slowly subsided.  However, rain continued into Tuesday across the region and each high tide during the period brought a reoccurrence of coastal flooding and erosion to the area.  Power outages persisted, and stream and river flooding continued across the region during this period.  Many roads remained closed.|On Friday, April 20, high pressure built eastward from the Great Lakes ending the influence of the Atlantic storm.  |  |Wind: The pressure gradient associated with the storm brought high winds to the region.  The damage observed in the hardest hit areas was typical of wind gusts of 60 to 80 mph.  While most observing sites reported winds below this range, topography, elevation, and exposure were likely factors in determining the amount of wind damage any location experienced.  In addition, the heavy rain brought strong wind gusts to the ground level and contributed to the sporadic nature of the heaviest wind damage.  In addition to the meteorological factors, damage from the wind was exacerbated because of the heavy rain that accompanied the wind and the soft, wet ground caused by the spring thaw.|The wind knocked over numerous trees and branches throughout the region and caused numerous and prolonged power outages throughout the region.| |Coastal Flooding/Storm Surge/Waves:  The coastal storm hit during a period of very high (and very low) astronomical tides.  In addition to the astronomical tides, the prolonged period of strong northeast winds caused a prolonged storm surge along the coastline.  Also during this period, the strong winds caused large and battering waves along the coast.  The storm tides and large waves caused significant flooding and coastal erosion. |In Portland, flood level is 12 feet.  During the storm, storm tides reached or exceeded the 12 foot flood level during 7 tidal cycles.  In addition, due to the large waves, coastal erosion occurred throughout the week of April 15th to 20th when the Portland gauge was above or near the 12 foot flood level.  Communication was lost with NOAA���s Portland Weather Buoy shortly after 6 am Monday when it was reporting 31 foot seas.|Precipitation:  Rain developed across the southern part of the state early Sunday afternoon, April 15th and spread northward.  The rain became heavy during the afternoon and overnight.  By Monday morning, 3 to 7 inches of rain had fallen in York County with rainfall amounts decreasing to 1 to 4 inches to the north and east.    In the mountains of Maine, 2 to 7 inches of snow fell by Monday morning.  Although the heaviest precipitation fell from Sunday afternoon into Monday afternoon, precipitation persisted into Tuesday.  Rainfall in Southern Maine was near the 100 year recurrence interval at Sanford and Eliot.|Flooding:  The heavy rain combined with snow melt to cause flooding of small rivers and streams in much of southern and central Maine.   The worst flooding occurred on the smaller rivers in York County.  Damage to infrastructure was severe (roads, bridges, waste water treatment plants, public buildings). Homes and businesses were also damaged. In York County, two people were killed when they attempted to cross a flooded road on foot and were swepted away. The crest on the Presumpscot River was just below the crest recorded during Hurricane Bob in August of 1991.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Tree down on car. Tree down on house. Numerous trees and power lines down.

event_description: Statewide state of emergency for the Patriots' Day Storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure rapidly intensified while tracking from the southeastern states to the southern New England coast from the 15th to the 16th. A tight pressure gradient developed between the low and high pressure centered over eastern Canada which also blocked the northern movement of the low. The intense low slowly drifted east from the 16th through the 19th while high pressure remained across eastern Canada. The storm had many impacts on the region including strong damaging winds...heavy rain with urban and small stream flooding and coastal tidal flooding. These impacts were most significant across Downeast areas...particularly near the coast. In addition...the storm brought locally heavy snow to some higher elevations of northern and northwest Maine.|The tight pressure gradient supported strong east to northeast winds across mostly central and Downeast portions of the region through the 16th and 17th. Disturbances rotating around the main low contributed to several surges of strong winds over the course of the event. Winds gradually diminished during the 18th and 19th...though gusty winds still lingered during this time particularly near the Downeast coast.|Damaging winds occurred across all of Downeast Maine...particularly near the coast where some wind gusts exceeded 70 mph. Damaging winds extended inland to central Piscataquis...central Penobscot and northern Washington counties. The combination of strong winds and saturated ground from the heavy rains which accompanied the storm and the spring thaw contributed to the uprooting of numerous trees with many other trees snapped and broken. Several trees fell on structures and vehicles causing damage. Other trees and branches brought down powerlines when they fell...with power poles also snapped and toppled due to the strong winds which contributed to thousands of power outages. Fallen trees and power lines also blocked roads.|The combination of astronomical high tides...amongst the highest of the year...along with persistent strong onshore winds and large waves contributed to coastal flooding during high tide cycles starting on the evening of the 16th and continuing through the evening of the 19th. During high tides...overwash flooded some coastal roads resulting in road closures. Debris was washed onto roads with some roads also damaged. A causeway connecting the mainland with Deer Isle was closed several times during the event due to overwash and flooding.|The storm also brought heavy rain to the region. The heaviest rains occurred across central and Downeast areas...along with the favored upslope areas of Piscataquis county. Rainfall totals across central and Downeast areas generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches...with local totals in excess of 5.00 inches. Across Piscataquis county...rainfall totals generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches with local totals approaching 5.00 inches. The heavy rain contributed to rapid rises on smaller rivers and streams across the region some of which overflowed onto surrounding low land areas. The small river and stream flooding caused some road closures. Urban and poor drainage flooding also occurred which led to additional road closures and contributed to basement flooding. Mainstem rivers also rose during this time but crested below flood stage.|Enough cold air was in place to support an interval of heavy snow during the early stages of the event across the higher terrain of Piscataquis county and northern Somerset county. Snowfall totals across some higher terrain areas ranged from 8 to 12 inches...with local totals in excess of 12 inches. Lesser snow acumulations occurred at lower elevations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds uprooted or broke numerous trees...along with snapping many branches across the region. Wind gusts of 45 to 55 mph were common...with some gusts to around 60 mph. Several intervals of particularly strong winds occurred. The first episode of stronger winds occurred during the afternoon of the 16th which produced the initial wind damage. The second episode of stronger winds...generally the strongest of the event...occurred during the night of the 16th producing further damage. The third episode of particularly strong winds occurred during the afternoon of the 17th. The uprooted trees and snapped branches falling on power lines...with many utility poles also toppled due to the winds...contributed to extensive power outages. Many roads were blocked due to fallen trees...utility poles and power lines. A tree fell on a vehicle in Dedham during the morning of the 17th injuring the driver.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure rapidly intensified while tracking from the southeastern states to the southern New England coast from the 15th to the 16th. A tight pressure gradient developed between the low and high pressure centered over eastern Canada which also blocked the northern movement of the low. The intense low slowly drifted east from the 16th through the 19th while high pressure remained across eastern Canada. The storm had many impacts on the region including strong damaging winds...heavy rain with urban and small stream flooding and coastal tidal flooding. These impacts were most significant across Downeast areas...particularly near the coast. In addition...the storm brought locally heavy snow to some higher elevations of northern and northwest Maine.|The tight pressure gradient supported strong east to northeast winds across mostly central and Downeast portions of the region through the 16th and 17th. Disturbances rotating around the main low contributed to several surges of strong winds over the course of the event. Winds gradually diminished during the 18th and 19th...though gusty winds still lingered during this time particularly near the Downeast coast.|Damaging winds occurred across all of Downeast Maine...particularly near the coast where some wind gusts exceeded 70 mph. Damaging winds extended inland to central Piscataquis...central Penobscot and northern Washington counties. The combination of strong winds and saturated ground from the heavy rains which accompanied the storm and the spring thaw contributed to the uprooting of numerous trees with many other trees snapped and broken. Several trees fell on structures and vehicles causing damage. Other trees and branches brought down powerlines when they fell...with power poles also snapped and toppled due to the strong winds which contributed to thousands of power outages. Fallen trees and power lines also blocked roads.|The combination of astronomical high tides...amongst the highest of the year...along with persistent strong onshore winds and large waves contributed to coastal flooding during high tide cycles starting on the evening of the 16th and continuing through the evening of the 19th. During high tides...overwash flooded some coastal roads resulting in road closures. Debris was washed onto roads with some roads also damaged. A causeway connecting the mainland with Deer Isle was closed several times during the event due to overwash and flooding.|The storm also brought heavy rain to the region. The heaviest rains occurred across central and Downeast areas...along with the favored upslope areas of Piscataquis county. Rainfall totals across central and Downeast areas generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches...with local totals in excess of 5.00 inches. Across Piscataquis county...rainfall totals generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.00 inches with local totals approaching 5.00 inches. The heavy rain contributed to rapid rises on smaller rivers and streams across the region some of which overflowed onto surrounding low land areas. The small river and stream flooding caused some road closures. Urban and poor drainage flooding also occurred which led to additional road closures and contributed to basement flooding. Mainstem rivers also rose during this time but crested below flood stage.|Enough cold air was in place to support an interval of heavy snow during the early stages of the event across the higher terrain of Piscataquis county and northern Somerset county. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong winds uprooted or broke trees...along with snapping many branches across the region. Wind gusts of 35 to 45 mph were common...with some gusts to around 60 mph. Nearly two dozen trees were uprooted in the Topsfield area alone over the course of the storm. The uprooted trees and snapped branches falling on power lines...with some utility poles also toppled due to the winds...contributed to power outages.

event_description: State of emergency for Aroostook County flooding on the St. John and Aroostook rivers

event_description: State of emergency for Aroostook County flooding on the St. John and Aroostook rivers

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A combination of 2.50 to 3.50 inches of rain and the melting of a record snowpack led to historic flooding of the Saint John River at Fort Kent. The Fish River which flows into the Saint John River at Fort Kent also overflowed its banks...contributing to the Fort Kent flooding. |The Saint John River initially began flooding in the vicinity of the juncture with the Fish River when the waters of the Saint John River backed up into the Fish River. event_description: Limited emergency declaration for power restoration crews ahead of the December 2008 ice storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm brought a mixture of snow, sleet, and freezing rain to Maine from the morning of December 11th to the morning of December 12th.  The greatest impact in the state was in coastal counties of the state where a significant ice storm occurred.  Following the ice storm, recovery and restoration efforts were negatively impacted by additional winter weather events that passed through the state.  ||The ice storm was caused by an area of low pressure that moved northeastward along a stalled frontal boundary off the East Coast.  Near ground level, cold air from eastern Canada funneled southward into the region on northerly winds.  Southerly winds at higher levels of the atmosphere brought warmer (above freezing) air in aloft.  Across southern sections of Maine, the thermal structure of the atmosphere was conducive to produce freezing rain and sleet event.   A mixture of snow, sleet, freezing rain and rain began Thursday morning across the state. However, as the northerly winds strengthened at the surface and southerly winds strengthened aloft, the precipitation changed to mostly a mix of sleet and freezing rain across western Maine.  The freezing rain and sleet continued overnight and into Friday morning before ending.  While ���melted��� precipitation amounts across much of southwestern and coastal Maine ranged from 1 to 3 inches, ice accretion to trees and wires in the coastal counties generally ranged from about a half inch to about an inch.  The weight of the ice caused branches to snap, and trees to either snap or uproot, and brought down power lines and poles across the region.  Hundred of thousands of utility customers lost power during the event, with some customers without power for more than a week.  Central Maine Power Company reported about 220,000 customers without power during height of the storm.  Total damages across western and mid coast Maine were estimated to be more than $13 million with most of the damage in coastal areas.

event_description: Limited emergency declaration for power restoration crews ahead of the December 2008 ice storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure tracking across Downeast Maine brought significant precipitation to all of northern and eastern Maine. Precipitation began during the afternoon of the 11th...then continued through the morning of the 12th. Enough warm air aloft was drawn across the region to allow the snow to transition to sleet and freezing rain. Across northern areas...storm total snow and sleet accumulations ranged from 3 to 5 inches with .25 to .50 of an inch of ice accumulation. Across central and Downeast areas...storm total snow and sleet accumulations ranged from 1 to 3 inches with .50 to 1.0 inch of ice accumulation. Numerous trees and power lines were toppled across the region due to the weight of the accumulated ice. Around 15000 customers lost power at various times during the event particularly across central and Downeast areas.|Strong onshore winds developed during the afternoon of the 12th along the Downeast coast...just south of the track of the low. Wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph were reported along the Downeast coast...with a peak gust of 63 mph at Sedgwick Ridge. The strong winds combined with the ice to contribute to downed trees and power lines. The strong onshore winds...along with an astronomically high tide...combined to produce minor coastal flooding near Winter Harbor at the time of high tide.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow and sleet accumulations ranged from 2 to 4 inches. Storm total ice accumulations were around 1/2 of an inch.

event_description: State of emergency letting power crews work longer hours after a windstorm left about 140,000 without power
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A tight pressure gradient between intense low pressure across southern New England and high pressure to the north produced strong east winds across Downeast Maine. The strongest winds occurred from the evening of the 25th into the early morning hours of the 26th. Wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph occurred across interior Downeast areas...with 60 to 70 mph gusts along the coast. |The combination of strong winds and wet ground led to thousands of trees being uprooted or snapped across the region. The most extensive tree damage was reported across southwest portions of Hancock county including Deer Isle...Stonington...Brooklin...Sedgwick...Blue Hill and Mount Desert Island. The falling trees brought down many power lines resulting in thousands of customers loosing power. The damage to the power infrastructure was extensive enough that in some locations power was not restored for several days. The falling trees also blocked many roads. In one instance...a tree fell on a parked unoccupied vehicle producing significant damage.|The low became nearly stationary across southern New England while several areas of moisture rotated around the low...producing areas of heavy snow across portions of northern Maine. The first round of heavy snow occurred from the overnight hours of the 24th into the 25th when 7 to 11 inches of accumulation were reported across  northern portions of Somerset and Piscataquis counties. A second interval of heavy snow occurred during the 26th affecting portions of northern Penobscot and northwest Aroostook counties. During this second event....7 to 12 inches of accumulation were reported across northwest Aroostook county with 5 to 9 inches across portions of northern Penobscot county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High winds toppled numerous trees and power lines across coastal Hancock county. The most extensive damage to trees and the power infrastructure occurred across the southwest corner of the county including Deer Isle...Stonington...Brooklin...Sedgwick...Blue Hill and Mount Desert Island. A 70 mph wind gust was reported at Brooklin with a 69 mph wind gust reported at Sedgwick Ridge.

event_description: State of Emergency Declaration
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Irene made landfall across western Long Island, NY and was downgraded to a Tropical Storm as it moved into and through New England.  The center of Irene was located just to the southwest of New Hampshire at 5 pm Sunday evening August 28 and then travelled up the Connecticut River Valley to the northern border of New Hampshire by 11 pm.  The storm brought a prolonged period of strong and gusty winds and heavy rain to Maine.  The high winds snapped or uprooted numerous trees throughout the state causing more than 300,000 customers to lose electrical and/or communication services.  The heavy rains caused rivers and streams in Western Maine to flood causing damage to bridges, roads, and property.||The strongest winds across the state began Sunday morning in southern areas and spread northward during the day.  The strong winds continued into the evening as the center of Irene moved through the Connecticut River Valley.  Winds continued to be gusty overnight as the storm moved away from the area. Observed maximum wind gusts included 56 mph at Augusta, 52 mph at Portland, 45 mph at Lewiston, and 44 mph at Fryeburg.  The combination of wet soil and the prolonged period of strong and gusty winds brought down numerous trees throughout the state.||Rainfall amounts across the state ranged from 1 to 3 inches along the coast to 3 to 7 inches across most of the remainder of western Maine with the heaviest precipitation falling in the mountains.  Rainfall was elevation dependant with the highest elevations receiving the greatest amounts.  In the mountains, much of the rain fell within a period of only several hours causing serious flash flooding of rivers and streams across Oxford, Franklin, and Somerset Counties.  Several bridges and roads were washed out or damaged by flash floods.  In addition, runoff from the heavy rains caused damage to nearby counties in western Maine.  Observed precipitation amounts included between 6 and 7 inches at Phillips and Andover, and between 5 and 6 inches at Temple, Kingfield, Sumner, and Hartford.   The Wild River at Gilead had a record crest of 17.42 feet with a corresponding flow of 36,848 cubic feet per second. ||Along the coast, the combination of high tides and large waves caused minor flooding, beach erosion, and splashover in the more vulnerable areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On Monday, October 29th, Hurricane Sandy (and its remnants) tracked northwest from well off the North Carolina coast to southeastern Pennsylvania, making landfall near the southern tip of New Jersey.  A band of heavy rain and high winds associated with Sandy moved northward into Maine Monday afternoon and continued moving northward through the State Monday night.  The high winds associated with this band of heavy rain downed numerous trees and caused widespread power outages, especially in southern areas.  In addition, the heavy rains caused some road washouts in the State. By Tuesday, the remnants of Sandy had moved into western Pennsylvania, but the circulation around the weakening storm continued to bring tropical air into the region during the day Tuesday and into Wednesday.  Localized heavy showers and thunderstorms developed in this tropical airmass Tuesday and Tuesday evening.  The shower activity diminished during the day Wednesday as cooler air moved into the region.||Winds across much of the State generally gusted from 40 to 70 mph late Monday afternoon and Monday night.  These strong and persistent winds combined with the powerful gusts to down numerous trees throughout the State and caused widespread power outages, especially across southern New Hampshire. A band of heavy rain and high winds associated with Sandy moved northward into Maine Monday afternoon and continued moving northward through the State Monday night.  The high winds associated with this band of heavy rain downed numerous trees and caused widespread power outages, especially in southern areas.  In addition, the heavy rains caused some road washouts in the State. By Tuesday, the remnants of Sandy had moved into western Pennsylvania, but the circulation around the weakening storm continued to bring tropical air into the region during the day Tuesday and into Wednesday.  Localized heavy showers and thunderstorms developed in this tropical airmass Tuesday and Tuesday evening.  The shower activity diminished during the day Wednesday as cooler air moved into the region.||Winds across much of the State generally gusted from 40 to 70 mph late Monday afternoon and Monday night.  These strong and persistent winds combined with the powerful gusts to down numerous trees throughout the State and caused widespread power outages, especially across southern New Hampshire.  Some peak wind gusts included 76 mph in Bath, between 60 and 70 mph in Portland and Kennebunk, and between 50 and 60 mph in Gray, South Bristol, Bristol, Saco, and Sanford.||The most significant hydrological impact from the storm was due to the band of heavy rain that fell between Monday afternoon and Tuesday morning.  Across the western part of the State, this band produced 1 to 3 inches of rain in about a 6- to 12-hour period with slightly higher amounts in the southeastern side of the mountains.  This amount of heavy rain in the short duration caused some road washouts in the region.  Minor flooding was also reported along the Swift River in Roxbury and along the Kennebec River at Skowhegan.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous trees were knocked over by the wind leading to widespread and prolonged power outages and road closures.  Central Maine Power reported more than 3700 customers with power outages countywide.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Sandy brought high winds and flooding to portions of east-central and Downeast Maine. The strongest winds generally occurred across Downeast areas from the late afternoon of the 29th into the early morning hours of the 30th. Sustained winds during this time generally ranged from 25 to 35 mph...with some gusts of 50 to 60 mph. The winds toppled trees and snapped branches. The falling trees and branches brought down power lines which contributed to power outages. Around 5500 customers lost power during the event...most extensive across Hancock county and southern portions of Penobscot county. A 50 foot barge was torn from its mooring and sunk at Bar Habor.|Heavy rains produced flash flooding and flooding across portions of Piscataquis county from the evening of the 30th into the afternoon of the 31st. Flash flooding developed across central and southern portions of Piscataquis county during the evening of the 30th. The flash flooding then transitioned to areal flooding from the early morning hours of the 31st through that afternoon. The mainstem of the Piscataquis River also flooded...cresting around a foot above flood stage at Dover-Foxcroft. Storm total rainfall across Piscataquis county generally ranged from 2.50 to 4.50 inches.

event_description: Limited civil emergency for a winter storm with heavy snow and high winds in southern and western Maine, to speed power restoration.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An area of low pressure developed rapidly off the Carolina coast late on the 7th and early on the 8th.  The storm moved very slowly northeast during the 8th and 9th as it continued to intensify.  By the morning of the 10th, the storm was located just to the east of Nova Scotia.  The storm brought heavy snow, high winds, and blizzard conditions to the state.  Snowfall amounts were generally 18 inches or more in coastal and interior zones where blizzard conditions caused considerable blowing and drifting snow.  In the mountains and foothills, snowfall amounts were in the 4 to 18 inch range.  Most of coastal Maine had blizzard conditions for 9 to 12 hours with interior areas reporting blizzard conditions for 3 to 10 hours.

event_description: Statewide emergency for arctic cold; hours-of-service relief for heating fuel drivers
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm located over the Mississippi Valley on the morning of the 14th moved northeast during the day.  A secondary low developed off the Mid-Atlantic coast and intensified rapidly by the morning of the 15th. event_description: Statewide emergency for an early winter storm with heavy wet snow and high winds; waiver for utility crews
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two areas of low pressure combined to produce heavy wet snow and high winds across Sagadahoc, Lincoln, Knox, Waldo, Kennebec, and southern Somerset Counties.  The first low produced mainly rain across the region Saturday night, but pulled colder air into the region from the north after it had passed.  The second low brought heavy wet snow during the day Sunday into Sunday evening. The weight of the wet snow and high winds caused numerous widespread and long-lasting power outages across the region. Several unofficial sites reported stronger wind gusts. event_description: State of Emergency after a severe wind and rain storm caused statewide power outages.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rapidly intensifying low pressure lifted across western New England during the 30th...with a boost from the remnants of what had been Tropical Storm Philippe.  A very tight pressure gradient between the low and high pressure to the east supported the development of a strong low level jet which crossed the region through the morning of the 30th in advance of a cold front. The strongest winds occurred during the morning of the 30th when south to southeast wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were common...with some gusts in excess of 70 mph. The strongest winds occurred in a region from Hancock county...southern and central Penobscot county...central and southern Piscataquis county into northern Somerset county. |The strong winds produced extensive tree damage in the area from Hancock county...across southern and central Penobscot county...southern and central Piscataquis county into northern Somerset county. The number of trees toppled...snapped or damaged is estimated in the hundreds of thousands. Leaves still on many trees and saturated ground contributed to the extensive tree damage. The falling trees and branches brought down power lines and snapped utility poles producing extensive damage to the electrical grid. Power outages began during the early morning hours of the 30th...then rapidly increased through the morning into early afternoon. Power outages within the EMERA Maine service area peaked at around 90,000 customers, which represented around 56% of their customer base. Power outages within the Eastern Maine Power service area peaked around 10,000 customers. The extensive damage to the electrical grid and number of snapped and uprooted trees hindered the recovery process. Roads blocked by fallen trees also slowed the recovery process. Full power was not restored until November 7th.|Trees falling on structures...vehicles and fences produced damage of varying degrees. The winds also produced roof and structural damage to shingles and siding. Signs were also bent or toppled. Damage to public infrastructure was estimated at $217,873 in Hancock county...$667,682 in Penobscot county and $68,396 in Piscataquis county. This damage...in addition to major damage across the remainder of the state...prompted a Disaster Declaration. Significant damage to private property also occurred, though monetary estimates were unavailable.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: High winds with a strong low level jet toppled and snapped numerous trees along with broken branches. The falling trees and branches produced extensive damage to the electrical grid snapping utility poles and downing power lines with widespread power outages. Wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph were common with peak wind gusts estimated at around 60 mph.

A strong low level jet crossed the region through the morning of the 17th in advance of the low. Along the Downeast coast...easterly winds were sustained at 30 to 40 mph with gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Across interior Downeast areas winds were sustained at 20 to 30 mph with gusts up to 50 to 60 mph.|The winds snapped or toppled numerous trees along with branches. The falling trees and snapped branches brought down power lines and utility poles. Power outages increased rapidly through the early morning hours of the 17th. Power outages peaked during the morning of the 17th at around 45000 customers across northern and eastern Maine. The most extensive power outages occurred across Hancock county...where nearly half of the power outages were reported. Downed tress blocking roads and the extent of damage slowed the recovery process. Power was not entirely restored across coastal portions of Hancock county until the 20th. The Deer Isle area was particularly impacted. Trees were reported snapped or toppled across much of Downeast Maine. However...damage was also concentrated around Acadia National Park where the falling trees prompted many road closures. Another area of concentrated damage was along Route 1...and side roads...in coastal Washington county where numerous reports of downed trees and power lines led to road closures.

event_description: Emergency proclamation to speed restoration of electrical power after the October 2019 wind and rain storm
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of October 15th a sharp upper trough dropped through the Upper Midwest, with surface low pressure moving into the Great Lakes. As the primary low pressure began to occlude on the 16th secondary low pressure development occurred on the Mid Atlantic coast. When the upper trough became negatively tilted the secondary low pressure rapidly deepened and tracked through New England overnight into the morning of the 17th. Low pressure ultimately bottomed out at 972 mb. Prior to the secondary low pressure occluding a strong low level jet lifted northeast across the coast of New England with strong wind gusts overnight on the 16th into the 17th.  Uprooted and snapped trees along with downed limbs caused significant power outages along coastal Maine.  Total power outages for the event in the state peaked around 200,000 customers without power.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong wind gusts in the early morning hours of the 17th led to downed trees and power lines across Knox County. Local mesonet weather stations measured wind gusts ranging between 45 and 60 mph, including a 58 mph wind gust at Knox County Regional Airport. Across Maine nearly 200,000 power outages were reported.

event_description: Proclamation of Emergency for Hurricane Lee.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Lee transitioned to a post-tropical cyclone while approaching the region. The storm made landfall in extreme southwest Nova Scotia during the afternoon of the 16th...near Long Island...before lifting across New Brunswick. The lowest pressure measured across northern and eastern Maine was 981.3 mb at Eastport in extreme southeast Washington county. A large wind field accompanied the storm...which impacted much of northern and eastern Maine. The highest wind gust also occurred in Eastport...closest to the point of landfall...measured at 54 knots (62 mph) during the morning of the 16th. The highest marine wind report was measured at 55 knots (63 mph) at the Jonesport buoy...also during the morning of the 16th. Wind gusts south of a line from southern Aroostook to central Piscataquis counties generally ranged from 39 to 48 knots (45 to 55 mph) through the morning into the afternoon of the 16th. Wind gusts across the remainder of northern and northwest Maine generally ranged from 30 to 39 knots (35 to 45 mph). These winds snapped branches and brought down many trees across northern and eastern Maine. The fallen trees and branches brought down power lines which contributed to power outages. No structural damage was reported across the region due to winds. A falling tree which smashed through the window of a van injured the driver.|Heavy rain accompanied the storm. The greatest rain totals occurred in southeast Washington county where local totals exceeded 6.00 inches...with a maximum total of 6.50 inches near Steuben. Localized flash flooding occurred in this area along with damage to roads and flooded basements. A sharp gradient of lesser rainfall occurred north and west of this region...with generally 2.00 to 4.00 inches on a line from northern Washington to Hancock counties. Totals of 1.00 to 2.00 inches occurred on a line from southern Aroostook to southern Penobscot counties. Totals northwest of this line were generally less than an inch.|Coastal flood impacts were minimal due to the strong offshore winds. The offshore winds mitigated coastal flood impacts during the several high tide cycles which occurred during this event. A rogue wave capsized a lobster boat off the coast of Hancock county injuring 2 on board.  A whale watch vessel broke from its mooring and ran aground. This led to the release of 1800 gallons of fuel...creating a HAZMAT incident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Post-Tropical Cyclone Lee produced 4.00 to 6.00 inches of rain which led to localized flash flooding. Brickyard Road in Pembroke was closed due to 6 to 10 inches of standing water on the road.

event_description: Proclamation of Emergency for Hurricane Lee.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hurricane Lee was a category 1 hurricane as it traveled north through the eastern Gulf of Maine early on Saturday, September 16th, before it was reclassified as Post-Tropical Cyclone Lee during the morning hours. The storm center eventually made landfall near Long Island, Nova Scotia on the evening of September 16th and then again in New Brunswick later on Saturday night. Lee brought numerous wind gusts of 35 to 50 mph across western Maine, which result in several downed trees and power outages.  Power outages in the GYX area of responsibility peaked around 125,000 outages.  There was one fatality as a large tree limb fell on a motorist.  Majority of power outages were in coastal Maine.  Rainfall amounts were mostly light, except along the Mid-coast, where amounts of 1 to 2 inches were reported.  There was no storm surge inundation coastal flooding with this event, with peak storm surge of around 2.5 that occurred at low tide on Saturday morning during a low astronomical tide cycle period.  Some very minor beach erosion occurred on Saturday afternoon due to the large nearshore waves.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Minor impacts were reported for this event.  No inundation flooding was reported, but there was high surf on the Saturday midday high tide cycle as long period 8 to 10 foot swells reached the coast.  This caused some minor splash-over and erosion in isolated areas.  Northerly wind gusts around 50 mph led to minor to moderate wind impacts as branches and many trees came down, which led to 7000 outages in the county on Saturday afternoon.  Power outage rates reached close to 25% of the county.  A man was killed while driving when a large tree limb fell on his car.  No flooding impacts were reported with rainfall amounts of 1 to 2 being reported.

event_description: Proclamation of State of Civil Emergency to facilitate recovery from a severe storm with heavy rainfall, high winds and flooding in Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Kennebec, Knox, Lincoln, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Sagadahoc, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure began organizing in the Gulf of Mexico on the 16th, setting record low sea level pressures as it traversed the Southeast through the 17th. Strong high pressure over the North Atlantic created a deep southeasterly flow that drew warm air into New England ahead of the approaching storm. By the time precipitation arrived on the evening of the 17th, temperatures were warm enough for rain everywhere except the highest peaks. Early on the 18th a shortwave trough was approaching from the Great Lakes and led to rapid deepening of the low pressure as it paralleled the Eastern Seaboard. Even as the center of the storm remained near Chesapeake Bay on the morning of the 18th, a strong low level jet had developed and winds began to gust in excess of 50 mph well inland from the coast. Damaging wind gusts continued into the afternoon. Hundreds of thousands of customers lost power due to falling limbs and downed wires. The anomalously warm air mass also led to intense rainfall rates beginning on the evening of the 17th, which continued into the 18th. Upsloping winds also enhanced precipitation along the southeast facing slopes of the mountains. Widespread 3 to 4 inches of rain fell, with isolated pockets of 6 to 8 inches. This fell on top of snow that was ripe from previous rainfall about a week earlier. An additional 2 to 3 inches of snow water equivalent was likely added to rainfall runoff. Numerous road washouts and road closures occurred due to flash flooding and fast responding small stream and tributaries. Widespread moderate to major flooding occurred along mainstem rivers.  The storm destroyed 13 homes, caused major damage to 106 others, with an additional 65 homes receiving minor flood damage.  Private damage was in the millions with public infrastructure damage of 20+ million being reported by FEMA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain and snowmelt caused the Sabattus River to flood Route 126 up to 4 feet deep. One water rescue was conducted due to people trapped in a vehicle.

Further upstream in Livermore, Goding Road near the Route 4 bridge was flooded, including Spruce Mountain Road.

Flooding was less severe on the east bank where most of the inundation was in recreational areas and portions of Howard Street.

The floodwaters reached levels near, above, and just below high-water marks from the flood of 1987, though that flood had un-natural responses due to complications from river ice.  Though streamflows were likely less than that of 1987, the reported damage was worse.  The hardest hit part of the community was in town near the Kowloon Village and Bethel Wastewater Treatment facility, and north of the river along Interval Road and Route 2 & 5. Further downstream in Hanover, flooding was extensive including inundation at the town office off Route 2.  About 7 businesses in Bethel sustained major flood damage.  The cost of the damage to roads and infrastructure was estimated at $1 million. There were over a dozen homes damaged by flood water with a total cost estimated around $750,000.

In Mexico numerous buildings flooded along Main Street, and properties off Canton Point Road in Peru. In Canton the flood waters entered buildings along Pleasant Street. There was at least home was destroyed and another 20-30 damaged by flood water with a total cost estimated around $2 million. About 2 dozen businesses between Rumford and Livermore sustained major flood damage.

event_description: Proclamation of State of Civil Emergency to facilitate recovery from a severe storm with heavy rainfall, high winds and flooding in Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Kennebec, Knox, Lincoln, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Sagadahoc, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties.
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure began organizing in the Gulf of Mexico on the 16th, setting record low sea level pressures as it traversed the Southeast through the 17th. Strong high pressure over the North Atlantic created a deep southeasterly flow that drew warm air into New England ahead of the approaching storm. By the time precipitation arrived on the evening of the 17th, temperatures were warm enough for rain everywhere except the highest peaks. Early on the 18th a shortwave trough was approaching from the Great Lakes and led to rapid deepening of the low pressure as it paralleled the Eastern Seaboard. Even as the center of the storm remained near Chesapeake Bay on the morning of the 18th, a strong low level jet had developed and winds began to gust in excess of 50 mph well inland from the coast. Damaging wind gusts continued into the afternoon. Hundreds of thousands of customers lost power due to falling limbs and downed wires. The anomalously warm air mass also led to intense rainfall rates beginning on the evening of the 17th, which continued into the 18th. Upsloping winds also enhanced precipitation along the southeast facing slopes of the mountains. Widespread 3 to 4 inches of rain fell, with isolated pockets of 6 to 8 inches. This fell on top of snow that was ripe from previous rainfall about a week earlier. An additional 2 to 3 inches of snow water equivalent was likely added to rainfall runoff. Numerous road washouts and road closures occurred due to flash flooding and fast responding small stream and tributaries. Widespread moderate to major flooding occurred along mainstem rivers.  The storm destroyed 13 homes, caused major damage to 106 others, with an additional 65 homes receiving minor flood damage.  Private damage was in the millions with public infrastructure damage of 20+ million being reported by FEMA.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Major to near record flooding occurred on the Kennebec River following heavy rain and snowmelt on December 18th. Heavy rain fell across the entire Kennebec Valley, however it was the combination of rain and snowmelt runoff in the mountains that caused catastrophic flooding across the region. Route 201 flooded in West Forks and just south of the confluence of the Kennebec River and Dead River. Flooding continued down to Caratunk where campgrounds and cabins along the rivers sustained substantial damage.

The rain fell over an 18 hour period and averaged 5 inches across the basin, with an additional 2 to 3.5 inches of snowmelt.  The steep terrain and frozen ground supported rapid runoff with all streams becoming raging torrents. The USGS river gage on the Carrabassett River in North Anson climbed from 5 feet to 26.64 feet in 24 hours, narrowly missing the all time record stage of 26.66 feet set in 1987.
